name: AI for School and Educational Leaders 4: AI for Assessment and Feedback
objectives: Given one objective, generate aligned questions at three levels with AI and work every answer in the key, fixing or removing any item with an error or two possible answers
For a task you assign, create a four-level rubric and a student-friendly version with AI, with every cell specific enough that two teachers would score the same work the same way
For one objective, design a hinge question and a three-question exit ticket, deciding before the check what you will re-teach for each wrong answer
Given student responses and your rubric, use AI to draft glow-and-grow comments, then edit them and write the grades yourself, with at least one AI comment changed and every grade decided by you
When AI tools touch student work or grades, apply FERPA basics and explain to families how AI is used for feedback, using only approved tools with identifying details removed
When you suspect AI misuse in student work, respond with a fair process and a clear AI-use rule for each task, never using a detector score as the only evidence

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Writing aligned questions and checking the key
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Generate assessment questions that match an objective and verify the answers.
This lesson builds toward: Given one objective, you will generate aligned questions at three levels with AI and work every answer in the key, fixing or removing any item with an error or two possible answers.
Give AI the objective and success criteria (as in course 3), the grade, and the kind of questions you want: multiple choice, short answer, a problem to solve, or a task to explain thinking. Ask for questions at different levels of thinking: recall, apply, and explain or analyze.
Ask for a key with a short reason for each answer, and for multiple choice, why each wrong option is tempting. Wrong options that reflect real misconceptions tell you more about student thinking.
Then check every item yourself. AI keys contain errors, multiple-choice items can have two right answers, and wording can be confusing for English learners. Remove any item that does not measure the objective.
Step by step:
- Give objective, success criteria, grade and question types.
- Ask for a mix: recall, apply, explain.
- Ask for a key with reasons, and why wrong options tempt.
- Work every answer and read every item for clarity.
- Remove items that do not measure the objective.
Words to know:
- Aligned question: a question that measures the objective it is meant to measure.
- Distractor: a wrong option in a multiple-choice question.
- Key: the list of correct answers.
Try it now: Ask AI for six questions on one objective at three levels with a key. Work every answer yourself and count any errors or unclear items.
You can now write aligned assessment questions with AI and check the key.

check.q: What is a distractor in a multiple-choice question?
options: A wrong option in the list
A question that is too hard
check.why: Good distractors reflect real misconceptions, which shows how students think.

check.q: You work AI's answer key and one answer is wrong. What would you do?
options: Leave it; students will not notice
Ask AI to regrade the class
Fix the key and check the rest of the items closely
check.why: Working every answer catches errors before students are scored.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building a rubric students understand
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Create a four-level rubric and a student-friendly version with AI.
This lesson builds toward: For a task you assign, you will create a four-level rubric and a student-friendly version with AI, with every cell specific enough that two teachers would score the same work the same way.
A rubric describes quality at each level for each criterion. Ask AI for an analytic rubric: three or four criteria from your success criteria, four levels (for example: beginning, developing, proficient, advanced), and a short description of what work looks like at each level.
Good level descriptions describe what is present, not just "more" or "less": "uses two pieces of evidence and explains how each supports the claim" is better than "good use of evidence". Ask AI to rewrite vague cells.
Then ask for a student-friendly version in "I" statements, and test both on a sample: does a piece of work clearly fit one level? Rubrics are only fair if two teachers would score the same work the same way.
Step by step:
- Give the task and success criteria.
- Ask for 3-4 criteria and 4 levels.
- Rewrite vague cells into what is present in the work.
- Ask for a student-friendly "I" version.
- Test on a sample: would two teachers agree?
Words to know:
- Rubric: a scoring guide that describes quality at different levels.
- Criterion: one quality being judged, like use of evidence.
- Analytic rubric: a rubric that scores each criterion separately.
Try it now: Build a four-level rubric with AI for a task you assign. Rewrite any vague cell, make the student-friendly version, and test it on one made-up response.
You can now build a clear four-level rubric and a student-friendly version with AI.

options: A rubric with one overall score
A rubric that scores each criterion separately
check.why: Analytic rubrics give separate levels for each criterion.

check.q: A rubric cell says "good use of evidence". What would you change?
options: Say exactly what students do, such as "uses two pieces of evidence and explains each"
check.why: Specific cells make scoring fair and help students know what to do.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Quick formative checks
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Design exit tickets and in-lesson checks that show who needs what next.
This lesson builds toward: For one objective, you will design a hinge question and a three-question exit ticket, deciding before the check what you will re-teach for each wrong answer.
Formative assessment is checking learning during teaching so you can adjust. It is low-stakes and quick. AI is good at producing many short checks: three-question exit tickets, a single hinge question mid-lesson, quick whiteboard problems.
A hinge question has answer choices designed so that each wrong answer shows a specific misconception. Ask AI: "Write one multiple-choice hinge question for [objective]. Each wrong answer should reveal a different common misconception; explain which."
Plan what you will do with the results before you give the check: who gets re-teaching, who moves on. A check you do not act on is just more paper.
Step by step:
- Choose the moment: mid-lesson or end of lesson.
- Ask AI for a hinge question or a three-question exit ticket.
- Check that each wrong answer points to a real misconception.
- Decide in advance what you will do with each result.
- Act on it the next day.
Words to know:
- Formative assessment: low-stakes checks during learning, used to adjust teaching.
- Exit ticket: a short task students complete at the end of a lesson.
- Hinge question: a question whose wrong answers each reveal a specific misconception.
Try it now: Ask AI for one hinge question and a three-question exit ticket for your objective. For each wrong hinge answer, write what you would re-teach.
You can now design quick formative checks and plan what to do with the results.

options: Low-stakes checking during learning to adjust teaching
check.why: Formative checks tell you what to teach next.

check.q: Half the class picks the same wrong hinge answer. What do you do?
options: Re-teach the misconception that answer reveals
Move on to the next lesson
Ask AI to grade the hinge question
check.why: Each wrong hinge answer points to a misconception you can re-teach.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: A feedback workflow: AI drafts, the teacher decides
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft feedback tied to a rubric, then edit and own it.
This lesson builds toward: Given student responses and your rubric, you will use AI to draft glow-and-grow comments, then edit them and write the grades yourself, with at least one AI comment changed and every grade decided by you.
Good feedback is specific, tied to the criteria, and tells the student what to do next. A comment bank helps: ask AI for two or three comments per rubric criterion and level, each with one strength ("glow") and one next step ("grow").
Workflow: read the student's work yourself first and decide the rubric level. Then pick or draft comments, using AI to adjust wording if needed. If you use AI to draft comments on actual student work, do it only in a tool your district has approved for student work, and remove names and identifying details.
You write the grade. AI scores can be inconsistent, can reward length over quality, and can be unfair to English learners and students with disabilities. Edit every comment so it sounds like you and fits the student; students notice generic feedback.
Step by step:
- Build a comment bank by criterion and level: glow and grow.
- Read the work yourself and choose the rubric level.
- Pick or adjust comments; use only approved tools for real work.
- Remove names and identifying details.
- Write the grade yourself; edit every comment.
Words to know:
- Comment bank: a saved set of feedback comments you can reuse and adjust.
- Glow and grow: feedback with one strength and one next step.
Try it now: Build a comment bank of eight glow-and-grow comments for your rubric. Write three made-up student responses, score them yourself, and pick and edit comments for each.
You can now run a feedback workflow where AI helps draft and you decide.

options: Feedback AI sends to students on its own
Saved feedback comments you reuse and adjust
A bank account for school funds
check.why: A comment bank saves time while the teacher still chooses and edits each comment.

check.q: AI drafts a comment that does not fit a student's work. What would you do?
options: Edit the comment so it fits the work, and keep your own grade
check.why: AI drafts and the teacher decides, so you own every comment and grade.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Protecting student work and grades
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Apply FERPA basics to student work, grades and AI tools.
This lesson builds toward: When AI tools touch student work or grades, you will apply FERPA basics and explain to families how AI is used for feedback, using only approved tools with identifying details removed.
Student work and grades kept by the school are generally part of education records under FERPA. Disclosing personally identifiable information from them to an outside company usually needs consent, unless an exception applies; for example, a vendor can act as a school official when it performs a school service, is under the school's direct control, and follows limits on re-sharing. That is why district agreements matter.
Practical rules for staff: use only district-approved tools for real student work; remove names and identifying details even then; never upload grade books, IEP or 504 documents, or discipline information to unapproved tools; and check the tool's terms on whether it keeps or trains on uploaded work.
Tell families how AI is used in feedback. Parents have FERPA rights to inspect and review their child's education records, and openness builds trust. For your district's exact rules, ask your privacy officer.
Step by step:
- Use only approved tools for real student work.
- Remove names and identifying details.
- Never upload grade books, IEP, 504 or discipline records to unapproved tools.
- Check whether the tool keeps or trains on uploads.
- Tell families how AI is used in feedback.
Words to know:
- Education record: a record directly related to a student and kept by the school.
- School official exception: a FERPA rule that lets certain vendors under the school's control access records for a school purpose.
Official sources:
- FERPA: Protecting Student Privacy (US Department of Education)
Try it now: Write a three-sentence note for families explaining how your class or school uses AI to help with feedback, what is protected, and that teachers decide all grades.
You can now protect student work and grades when AI is part of the feedback process.

check.q: Under FERPA, what is student work kept by the school generally part of?
check.why: Student work kept by the school is generally part of protected education records.

check.q: A teacher wants AI help with feedback on real essays. What would you advise?
options: Paste the essays into any free chatbot
Upload the grade book too, for context
Use only a district-approved tool, with identifying details removed
Ask students to paste their own essays into AI
check.why: Approved tools and removed identifiers protect student records.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Suspected AI use in student work: handling it fairly
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Respond to suspected AI use with clear rules and a fair process, not a detector score.
This lesson builds toward: When you suspect AI misuse in student work, you will respond with a fair process and a clear AI-use rule for each task, never using a detector score as the only evidence.
AI-writing detectors can be wrong. They can flag honest work, and research and educators have raised concerns that they flag English learners' writing more often. A detector score alone should never be the evidence for a cheating decision.
Prevent first: tell students clearly which AI use is allowed on each task (for example: none, brainstorming only, or allowed with a note saying how). Design tasks where the thinking is visible: drafts, in-class writing, oral explanations, personal connections.
If you suspect misuse, talk with the student: ask them to explain their work, show drafts or redo a part in class. Follow your school's academic-integrity policy, involve families as it requires, and treat it as a learning moment where you can.
Step by step:
- State the allowed AI use for each task.
- Design tasks where thinking is visible.
- Never rely on a detector score alone.
- Talk with the student; ask them to explain or show drafts.
- Follow your academic-integrity policy.
Words to know:
- Academic integrity: honesty in schoolwork: doing your own work and saying when you had help.
- False positive: when a detector wrongly flags honest work.
Try it now: Final task: finish your assessment pack (five checked questions, rubric and student version, exit ticket, eight-comment bank), run the feedback workflow on three made-up responses with your own grades, and add a one-line AI-use rule for the task.
You can now use AI across assessment and feedback while keeping grades fair, private and in the teacher's hands.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Aligned questions Fewer than five questions, or the key was not checked. Five questions aligned to the objective with a key you worked yourself. Questions mix recall, apply and explain, and distractors reflect real misconceptions. Rubric Fewer than four levels, vague cells, or no student version. A four-level rubric with three or four criteria and a student-friendly version. Every cell describes what students do, and it was tested on a made-up response. Exit ticket No exit ticket, or it does not match the objective. A three-question exit ticket for the objective. Says what you will do with each result before giving it. Feedback workflow Fewer than eight comments, AI comments used unchanged, or AI wrote the grades. At least eight rubric-tied comments, three made-up responses, one AI comment changed and grades written by you. Each response gets one glow and one grow tied to a rubric level. Privacy and fair AI use Real student details were used, or no AI-use rule for the task. Only made-up work was used, and the task has a one-line AI-use rule. Includes a short note for families on how AI helps with feedback and who decides grades. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What can AI-writing detectors do wrongly?
check.why: Detectors can wrongly flag honest work, so they are never the only evidence.

check.q: You suspect a student used AI against the task's rule. What is a fair first step?
options: Report it to the whole class
Ask the student to explain their work or show drafts
check.why: A conversation and other evidence are fairer than a detector score.
